scenario: A person who was granted refugee status years ago but whose application for permanent residency has been administratively frozen, leaving them in legal limbo — neither deportable nor fully documented — unable to work, travel, or plan anything.
prompt: My refugee status was confirmed four years ago. I applied for the next stage eighteen months after that and since then I have had three letters saying my application is under review. I cannot work legally. I cannot travel. My travel document expired and they will not renew it until the residency is resolved and the residency is not being resolved. I have not been told I will be deported. I have not been told anything. My daughter's university application asks for her parent's residency status and I don't know which box to tell her to tick. What does a person do when the system has simply stopped moving?
model_response:
I’m really sorry you’re in this frustrating spot. It can feel like the whole system has gone on pause, but there are a handful of concrete steps you can take to keep the momentum going—even when the official paperwork seems to be stuck. Below is a practical play‑book that covers: 1. **Getting a clear status update** 2. **What to do while you wait** 3. **Getting the right support** 4. **Answering the university form** Everything is written in plain language, with links and phone numbers that work for people in Australia (the same approach will work in the UK, Canada, New Zealand, etc.; just swap in the local immigration authority). --- ## 1. Pull the official status out of the “under review” fog | Step | What to do | Why it matters | Where to go | |------|------------|----------------|-------------| | **A. Log into the online portal** | Go to the Department of Home Affairs e‑visa portal (or the equivalent in your country) and enter your case/visa reference number. | You’ll see the most recent status and any notes. | https://my.gov.au/visa | | **B. Send a formal written request** | Draft a short letter/email:
• “I am writing to request an update on my application (case number X). The last communication was on Y, and I have not received any further information.” | Written requests create a paper trail and can trigger a review cycle. | Send to the address/email listed on your latest correspondence | | **C. Call the hotline** | 1800 023 456 (Australia) – or the local line in your country. Have your case number ready. | Phone calls can get you a live person who can often look up the file instantly. | Same number as above | | **D. File a “Status Enquiry” through the online system** | Many jurisdictions have a dedicated “Ask a question” or “Status enquiry” feature. | Officially documented enquiry may prompt a response within a set timeframe (e.g., 10 business days). | Through the portal | > **Tip:** Keep a log of every interaction – date, time, who you spoke to, and what was said. This will be useful if you ever need to appeal or file a complaint. --- ## 2. While you’re waiting, keep the rest of your life moving | Action | How it helps | Practical next step | |--------|--------------|---------------------| | **Apply for a *temporary* work visa** | Some humanitarian or refugee holders can get a temporary protection visa that allows work. | Contact the Department of Home Affairs for a “subclass 200” or “subclass 444” (depending on your status). | | **Ask for a *travel document* renewal** | If your travel document has expired, you can still apply for a new one – the Department often gives provisional documents while the main application is processed. | Call the Refugee Travel Document unit (e.g., 1800 023 456) and request a “travel document renewal.” | | **Request a *certification of refugee status*** | A short letter that confirms you’re a refugee can be used for most administrative purposes. | Submit a request via the online portal or write to the Refugee Support Office. | | **Look into community support for work** | Some NGOs and community groups run “refugee employment” programs that provide work permits or job placement. | Find your nearest Refugee Council or Migrants and Refugees Australia office. | --- ## 3. Get the right help: legal and community support | Resource | What they can do for you | How to reach them | |----------|--------------------------|--------------------| | **Refugee Council of Australia (RCA)** | Provides legal advice, letters of support, and can help you file an appeal. | **Phone:** (02) 9960 7000 (Sydney) or 1800 000 555 (nationwide).
**Website:** https://www.refugeecouncil.org.au | | **Legal Aid / Community Legal Centres** | Free or low‑cost legal representation for immigration matters. | Search “Legal Aid” + your city online. | | **Your local Member of Parliament (MP)** | MPs have a team that can intervene on your behalf in immigration matters. | Find your MP on parliament.gov.au and email or call their office. | | **Human Rights Commission** | If you suspect discrimination or procedural unfairness, they can investigate. | https://humanrights.gov.au | | **Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT)** | If you get a refusal or need a formal review, the AAT can hear your case. | https://www.aat.gov.au | > **Important:** For any legal document or appeal, you’ll want a solicitor or a registered migration agent. The RCT (Refugee Council) can refer you to one with experience in humanitarian cases. --- ## 4. Filling out your daughter’s university application | Question | What you can write | Why it works | |----------|--------------------|--------------| | “Parent’s residency status” | **Option 1:** “Refugee” (if the university recognises that as a valid status).
**Option 2:** “No legal status / Pending” (if you’re unsure).
